newsitem.title: USA: Congress urged to allow electric utility competition.
newsitem.headline: Congress urged to allow electric utility competition.

text.p: Businesses and consumers Monday urged Congress to allow competition in the $200 billion electric industry, but residential customers and utilities expressed concern about how deregulation should take place.

"Economists tell us that bringing consumer choice to electricity saves the average household between 15 and 42 percent over a period of time off their electric bill," House Commerce Energy and Power Subcommittee Chairman Dan Schaefer said at the opening of a public hearing on restructuring the electric utility industry.
Schaefer, a Colorado Republican, said the federal government is the biggest consumer of electricity in the country, spending $3.5 billion a year.
The hearing was the first of four public sessions in cities across the country.

Small business owners complained about wide disparities in electric rates. Tony Fitzpatrick of Wayfield Foods, which has nine grocery stores in predominantly black Atlanta neighbourhoods, said his rates varied 59 percent, depending on the electricity supplier.
"I know of no supermarket in America that could get away with prices 59 percent higher than their competitors' down the street and still stay in business," he said.

Florist shop owner Leone Grizzard said high electric rates in the Atlanta suburb of East Point put a nearby soul food restaurant out of business and have caused her electric bills to triple since 1989.
Representatives of Home Depot Inc. and Procter & Gamble Co. also urged competition.

"The federal government must provide a date certain by which all consumers are allowed to choose their electricity suppliers because the states are not moving forward fast enough to open electricity markets," said Jim Lair, corporate manager of energy programmes for Atlanta-based Home Depot.
But Hans Spakovsky, a homeowner in suburban Sandy Springs, Ga., warned individual residential customers could be at a disadvantage.
"Deregulation must be accomplished in such a manner that residential consumers are not harmed by their weaker negotiating power and lack of sophistication in this area," he said.
An executive with the Southern Co., the parent company of five electric utilities serving 3.5 million people in the Southeast, said states should control the timing and details of retail competition.

Southern Co. Senior Vice President David Ratcliffe said competition could create disparities in utility taxation. He cautioned that state and local tax revenues could fall if the assessed value of utility property declines because of competition.

Raymond Sauer, a Clemson University economics professor, presented a study which said full customer choice could cause the average price of power to fall 13 percent to 25 percent in the short run and up to 42 percent in the long run.
